From Premium Consumption to Strategic Production:

Apple’s iPhone Strategy in Japan and India

 

1. Company Background

Apple Inc. is a California-based multinational technology corporation and manufacturer of consumer electronics and digital services founded in 1976 and headquartered in Cupertino, California, USA. The company is now being led by John Ternus following the announced leadership transition at Apple, and Tim Cook remains the Executive Chairman of the company. With a strong focus on branding and the quality of their products and services, Apple has developed a strong global presence with its integrated ecosystem and standardized customer experience across the international markets. Apple’s total revenue for fiscal year 2025 was nearly US$416 billion, distributed across its primary regional markets: the Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific (ROA). (Market Track 2025). But the iPhone has been Apple’s most aggressive and successful product, over half of Apple’s revenue comes from the iPhone, and it is the foundation of Apple’s international customer base and ecosystem (Smith 2025).

Standardisation and adaptation between countries is one of the main reasons for Apple’s success in marketing in the world (Qamara et al. 2025). The company has a very standardised identity, operating and communicating on a global level, using consistent product design, positioning, brand communication and operating systems. But Apple customises some of the marketing elements as per the local market conditions, such as pricing measures, retail relationships, financing options, distribution networks and communication plans. The ratio helps Apple have a consistent brand image worldwide but be able to tailor itself to the different markets and their different purchasing power and maturity.

The focus of this report is on the iPhone as it is Apple’s biggest revenue generator and a product that has had the biggest impact on international growth. The parallels between Japan and India are used to explore how Apple can use the same global brand identity but apply the tenets of global marketing in different ways to a mature premium market and an emerging, stratified market.

1. Comparison of International Markets: Japan and India

  1. PESTEL Model and Criteria

To compare the performance of Apple’s iPhone in Japan and India, this report applies the PESTEL framework as the primary theoretical model for international market selection.

 

PESTEL is a suitable tool for this report, as a successful international strategy for the Apple product will rely on the product’s competitiveness but also the national environment that is influencing consumers’ demand and business operations. Politically and legally, government policies impact market access, manufacturing, taxation and retailing. Economics influence the purchasing power and consumer ability to purchase high quality items such as the iPhone. This includes social and technological factors, as there is a significant difference between the smartphone usage and the preference of consumers in different countries. However, PESTEL also has limitations. This framework focuses primarily on macroeconomic conditions and does not directly assess microeconomic conditions (Yuksel 2012). Furthermore, the PESTEL model may oversimplify consumer decision-making processes, as cultural values ​​and purchasing motivations are often more complex than broad environmental indicators.

Aside from the PESTEL model, the following three criteria were chosen for market comparison: purchasing power, population size and performance in the market. The inclusion of purchasing power was justified since high-end smartphones like the iPhone would only be used by people who have both the money and desire to buy high-tech gadgets. Population size was chosen to represent the overall size of the market, as well as its demographic makeup and the opportunities for customer acquisition in the long-term, and because differences in population characteristics are likely to affect market maturity and future growth. Lastly, Apple’s market performance was incorporated to assess what market situation Apple currently occupies, as well as its strategic position in each market.

Figure 2. Criteria Analysis

The PESTEL analysis is used as a theoretical basis in the selection of comparison criteria because it gives an explanation of the effect of the macro-environmental conditions on the attractiveness of the market and global marketing. While all the PESTEL dimensions are applied to Apple’s iPhone business model, this report concentrates on three of the most relevant: purchasing power, population characteristics and Apple’s market performance. The key criteria chosen reflect those with a direct bearing on the demand for ‘high quality’ consumer electronics and enable a meaningful comparison between a relatively developed international market and an emerging one.

The economic dimension of PESTEL is the most important dimension of PESTEL and is very relevant for Apple as the iPhones come in the category of premium smartphones. Japan and India have similar GDP (about US$4.38 trillion and US$4.15 trillion, respectively) but they are very different in terms of market attractiveness from the individual consumer. Japan’s GDP per capita at US$35,703 is significantly higher than India’s at US$2,813, meaning that people have a higher purchasing power and affordability of high-end devices. This will help boost Apple’s revenue per customer and its ability to charge high prices in Japan. But the attractiveness of an economy should not be judged solely by their ability to spend money. India’s GDP growth rate of 6.48% against 0.72% of Japan indicates more growth potential in the future with the rising income levels and growing middle class.

The social component of PESTEL is used to inform the population characteristics and give extra insight into consumer demand. Japan’s population (approx. 123.4M) has an average age of 50.3, and it is an mature and ageing consumer market where consumers are buying smartphones out of the necessity to replace, quality and ecosystem loyalty. In India, though, there are approximately 1.46 billion people with a median age of 29.2, and a burgeoning young population with a high degree of digital adoption. Apple will have to balance premium positioning with reaching a larger market if this is the case as they will be dealing with higher price sensitivity among this demographic.

Lastly, the appeal of the market is reinforced by the performance of market players, which are based on the political, technological and competitive factors discussed in the PESTEL model. Overall, Japan is one of Apple’s most robust premium markets, with the company commanding some 59.65% of smartphone market share, which shows a high level of brand acceptance and consumer loyalty. In comparison, India is less attractive from a short-term premium consumption point of view as there is a lot of competition from lower-priced alternatives. However, India has gained prominence not just for being a market for consumer buying and selling but also in Apple’s international supply chain, accounting for about 25% of the world’s iPhone manufacturing. So, a comparison of Japan and India enables an evaluation of the relative merits of the Apple strategy of short-term profit with long-term strategic development in various international markets.

  1. Summary of Market Selection

The case of Japan vs. India shows that Apple chose these markets for their different roles in its global marketing mix. Japan is a mature nation with a high purchasing power (GDP per capita: US$35,703), high levels of brand loyalty and Apple’s smartphone market share of some 59.65%. Japan boasts a population of 123.4 million and a maturing smartphone market, which offers consistent sales of replacement units and demand for high-specification models.

India, on the other hand, is a growth market and not a premium consumption market. Despite the low level of purchasing power India has a large population (1.46 billion), a younger population age structure (median age: 29.2) and a relatively high economic growth rate (6.48%). In addition to consumer demand, India has also emerged as a strategic location due to its manufacturing capabilities, accounting for about 25% of the global production of iPhones (Phartiyal 2026). Thus, Apple’s footprint in both markets indicates a well-rounded distribution strategy focused on short-term profitability in established markets and building a long-term growth and supply chain resilience strategy in emerging markets.

1. Analysis of Apple’s Market Entry Method in India

The internationalisation of the Apple business model has been done through a controlled approach of direct investment, authorised distribution, and growing localisation of manufacturing capacities in India. Apple has shifted the focus from India as a premium consumer market to a potential growth market and a key production market in its supply chain. This is a higher control entry mode than licensing or franchising. The Dunning’s Eclectic Paradigm (OLI Framework) is used to assess this strategy. The main argument of the framework is that firms choose foreign market entry strategies depending on the ownership (O), location (L), and internalisation (I) advantages.

The company’s relative high operational control can be attributed to its ownership advantages. The competitive advantage of Apple relies on proprietary technology, positioning the brand as premium, and its integration with the ecosystem (Zhang and Hu 2024). Licensing and franchising would have lost control of the customer experience and the brand would have been less consistent. But the most attractive part of India is location. From a premium consumption perspective, India is less desirable than Japan, given that it has a lower GDP per capita (US$2,813 vs US$35,703), but it has the potential for significant production and growth. India has one of the world’s largest labour force, 678,6 million workers with a younger median age of 29.2 years (Malin and Tyagi 2023). Labour costs are still much cheaper than those in China. The average monthly wage of factory workers is between USD 150 and USD 300, and above USD 600 in China (I2W 2025). This outcome enabled Apple and its manufacturing partners to lower manufacturing costs, and keep up production volume.

The attractiveness of India has been further bolstered by its policy. The Indian government offers financial incentives and regulatory support to promote electronics manufacturing and foreign direct investment (FDI) through schemes like Production Linked Incentive (PLI) and the “Make in India” policies (NmK and Kalshan 2025). The policies generate these mutual benefits for Apple: lower production costs, reduced reliance on a single manufacturing geography, supply chain diversification, and employment creation, as well as for India: technology transfer, export expansion, and industrial development. By 2025 India will be manufacturing about 25% of iPhones in the world, thus moving away from China-centric manufacturing to a multi-country manufacturing model (Phartiyal 2026). At present, the strategic importance of this production function is greater to Apple than is direct consumer sales. But Apple’s investment plan also suggests future growth in the consumer market. The first Apple stores were opened in high income metropolitan cities where the demand for high quality electronics was seen, in India, namely Apple BKC Mumbai and Apple Saket New Delhi by Tandel et al. (2025). This selective market entry is an illustration of the income inequalities that prevail in India and the urban concentration of the purchasing power. Apple obviously isn’t aiming for instant market share across the country, it’s focused on predominant demand in more affluent city populations while slowly building demand for Apple’s premium devices as income levels and middle-class consumption continues to rise.

1. Analysis of Apple’s Marketing Strategies in Japan

The case of Apple in Japan highlights the importance of globalising while adapting selectively to the local market to enhance performance. Product adaptation and premium pricing are two successful strategies for Apple’s iPhone in Japan that make a major contribution.

Although the company has a very standardized product design worldwide, some product adaptations have been made to meet the Japanese consumer’s expectations and social norms. The Japanese iPhone camera system is one of the interesting examples in which the shutter sound is not completely silenced during photography (Oto 2024). This is a local concern about privacy protection, and social norms around public photographing, all of which has been a solid adaptation of smartphones sold in Japan. Apple makes local tweaks to selected functions, but doesn’t change the essence of the product. It is in line with the theory of selective adaptation as it states that there is a limited number of adjustments that can be made to facilitate market fit without adding too much complexity to the operation (Tsougkou et al. 2025).

Prices are also contributing to Apple’s high-end market presence in Japan. Rather than going with penetration pricing, Apple keeps prices high as it is an attempt to further drive home the idea of quality, innovation, and exclusivity. This approach is in line with the relatively high purchasing power of the Japanese people (US$35,703 GDP per capita) and the desire to invest in flagship technology products. Apple dominated the Japanese smartphone market with about 59.65%, indicating that high prices haven’t hurt sales. But even though the iPhone is the preferred, and willing-to-pay-for, line of phones in Japan, the Promax line is not the top choice. As reported by Counterpoint (2025), the top three devices for September 2025 were the iPhone 16e, the iPhone 16 and the iPhone 17 Pro, indicating that consumer demand for smartphones is high but is focussed on the usability of flagship devices rather than the most premium.
